history_of_present_illness: The disease typically begins as a papule or vesicle on the penis or labia minora. The lesion progresses, and the thin epidermal layer sloughs off, revealing a surface of granulations that bleed easily and discharge a creamy, often offensive substance. The process extends by continuity from the penis to the groins and down the inner thighs. Involvement of the glans penis may manifest as a fungating growth resembling epithelioma. In females, the disease spreads from the labia minora into the vagina, to the labia majora, and then to the perineum and perianal region, frequently resulting in recto-vaginal fistulae. Progression is more rapid and pronounced when invading mucous membranes. Concurrently with the advancing granulomatous process, there is often cicatrization of previously affected areas, forming scar tissue that readily breaks down. Patients experience little pain or itching, and their general health remains unimpaired. Lymphatic glands are not enlarged. While the process spreads by continuity, it can also pass to areas in contact with the diseased tissue. Healing tends to occur in affected skin, but not in mucous membranes, and there is minimal tendency toward ulceration.
exposure_and_epidemiology: Historically, Daniels first noted the disease in British Guiana in 1896, though Macleod had previously described it in India as “serpiginous ulceration of the genitals.” Cases have been chiefly reported from British Guiana and the West Indies, but it is now recognized in India, China, Northern Australia, various Pacific islands, and Northern and Central Africa. Grindon reported three cases from the United States. Etiologically, the disease is more prevalent in women than in men and is rarely observed before puberty. It is believed to be transmitted by sexual intercourse.
physical_exam: The disease initially presents as a papule or vesicle on the genitals. As it progresses, the affected areas develop granulations that are prone to bleeding and produce a creamy, frequently offensive discharge. On the glans penis, a fungating growth suggestive of epithelioma may be observed. In advanced cases, recto-vaginal fistulae can form. Previously invaded areas often show cicatrization, resulting in scar tissue that breaks down easily. There is no enlargement of the lymphatic glands. Pathologically, the process involves a small round cell infiltration of the superficial corium, with the growth being well vascularized. There is an abundance of plasma cells and a marked tendency toward fibrous tissue formation; giant cell formation and caseation are absent.
labs_and_diagnostics: Various spirochaetes have been reported in the lesions, though Wise's finding of spirochaetes resembling *Treponema pallidum* is not widely accepted. Donovan reported the presence of an oval bacillus (1½ × 2 microns) within large phagocytic cells in scrapings from ulcerations, often with several bodies per cell. Flu described a capsulated organism in plasma cells (and occasionally other cells), which he believed to be related to the Friedlander group, though his cultural work was inconclusive and it is likely a secondary invader. There is also a suggestion of a cellular reaction characteristic of chlamydozoa.
differential_diagnosis: The disease may be confused with a syphilitic process, but this is negated by the absence of gland involvement and secondary manifestations of syphilis. It can also be suggestive of tuberculous or epitheliomatous processes, particularly due to the fungating growth on the glans penis. Key distinguishing features include its marked chronicity and strong tendency toward scarring.
management_and_clinical_course: Excision of the entire granulomatous area, extending into normal skin, has been considered by some as the only cure. Ordinary antisyphilitic treatment appears to be ineffective, and reports of success with salvarsan may stem from misdiagnosis of a syphilitic process as granuloma venereum. Radiotherapy has been recommended. Local treatment involves antiseptic or deodorant washes or ointments. The standard treatment is Antimony Treatment, as reported by Breinl, using intravenous tartar emetic injections, similar to the treatment for leishmaniasis. Local compresses soaked with a ½% solution of tartar emetic are also recommended. The disease is characterized by chronicity, with a tendency for scarring, and while healing often occurs in affected skin, it does not typically occur in mucous membranes.
